n: Alma greets the church in Gideon warmly. It is his first time speaking to them in person, because his duties as chief judge had kept him busy.
He could only come now because he gave up the judgment seat, and he sees the chance to visit as the Lord’s mercy.

f.w: the judgment-seat hath been given to another

n: Alma came hoping to find them humble, prayerful, and blameless — not in the sad state he found in Zarahemla.

f.g: The perilous spiritual condition of the Zarahemla church.

n: He rejoices that the church in Zarahemla has now returned to righteousness.
Alma hopes to rejoice over Gideon too — but without the grief he went through in Zarahemla, where his joy came only after much sorrow.
He expresses trust that they are not proud, focused on riches, or worshiping idols, but are looking forward to Christ with lasting faith.

f.w: the true and the living God

n: Of all the things to come, one matters most: the Redeemer will soon live and come among his people.
Alma humbly admits what he doesn’t know: whether Christ will visit the Nephites during his mortal life. The Spirit hadn’t told him. (Christ later came to them after his resurrection.)
What the Spirit did say: call the people to repent and prepare the way of the Lord, for the Son of God is coming to earth.

f.w: prepare the way of the Lord

n: Alma prophesies that Christ will be born of a virgin named Mary, conceiving by the power of the Holy Ghost. “At Jerusalem” refers to the land of Jerusalem — Bethlehem lies just a few miles from the city.

f.w: at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers
f.g: Book of Mormon writers often say “land of Jerusalem” for the surrounding region.

n: Christ will suffer every kind of pain, affliction, and temptation, taking on himself his people’s pains and sicknesses — fulfilling Isaiah’s prophecy.

f.w: he will take upon him the pains and the sicknesses of his people

n: A profound verse on the Atonement: Christ takes on death to break its hold, and takes on our weaknesses so that he knows from experience how to help us. “Bowels” was the ancient idiom for the seat of compassion.

f.g: The inner self; in scripture, the source of deep feeling and compassion.

n: Though the Spirit knows all things, the Son of God suffers in the flesh so he can take upon himself his people’s sins and blot them out. This is Alma’s personal testimony.
Alma calls for rebirth and baptism, to be washed from sin and to have faith in the Lamb of God who takes away the world’s sins.
Come without fear, lay aside the sins that entangle you, and covenant with God through baptism to keep his commandments.

f.w: every sin, which easily doth beset you
enter into a covenant with him

n: Those who are baptized and keep the commandments will have eternal life — Alma bears witness by the Holy Spirit.
Alma perceives by the Spirit that the people believe, and their strong faith fills him with joy.
His hopes have been fulfilled: the people of Gideon are not in the troubled state of Zarahemla.
He sees that they are on the path to God’s kingdom, making his paths straight.
God never walks crooked paths or changes his word. His course is “one eternal round” — utterly consistent and trustworthy.
God does not dwell in unholy temples, and nothing unclean can enter his kingdom. At the last day the filthy remain filthy.

f.g: Can mean both buildings and our bodies.

f.w: he who is filthy shall remain in his filthiness

n: Alma explains why he spoke: to awaken them to their duty to God and help them walk blamelessly in the holy order they entered at baptism.
A portrait of Christlike character: humble, submissive, gentle, easy to approach, patient, temperate, diligent, prayerful for both spiritual and physical needs, and always grateful.

f.g: Approachable; willing to listen and be persuaded.

n: Have faith, hope, and charity, and good works will naturally follow.
Alma blesses them to keep their garments spotless so they may sit with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the prophets in heaven, never to leave.
Alma rejoices at how diligently they heeded his words.
He closes with a blessing of peace on their homes, lands, flocks, and families, according to their faith and works.
